rule: The English Wikipedia article sets the book on the atlas island. Inspired by, based on, and filmed on do not count. Summary sentences are the article's own.

rows.title: Coffin Road
rows.evidence: Published in the UK in 2016, Coffin Road is a standalone thriller set on the Isle of Harris.
rows.summary: Published in the UK in 2016, Coffin Road is a standalone thriller set on the Isle of Harris. The story has an ecological theme involving links between big pharmaceutical companies and colony collapse disorder in bees.

rows.title: The Killing Stones
rows.evidence: The Killing Stones (2025); Set in the Orkney Islands after the previous books.
rows.reject_reason: The Ann Cleeves article only has a bibliography line saying The Killing Stones is set in the Orkney Islands. It does not set the novel on Mainland, and the summary is that catalogue fragment rather than sentences placing the book on Mainland.
rows.summary: The Killing Stones (2025); Set in the Orkney Islands after the previous books.

rows.title: As It Was/Sin Mar a Bha: An Ulva Boyhood
rows.evidence: In 2000, D. W. R. MacKenzie wrote As It Was/Sin Mar a Bha: An Ulva Boyhood, which is a combination of autobiography and a potted history of the island.
rows.summary: In 2000, D. W. R. MacKenzie wrote As It Was/Sin Mar a Bha: An Ulva Boyhood, which is a combination of autobiography and a potted history of the island. rows.title: Herm, Our Island Home
rows.evidence: Jenny Wood, the wife of tenant Major Peter Wood, published her memoirs in 1986. Wood, Jenny, Herm, Our Island Home (Linton, 1986).
rows.reject_reason: The summary's sentences are about Fairy Gold, which the same paragraph calls a fictional portrayal, and about Jenny Wood publishing memoirs in 1986. They never name Herm, Our Island Home. The summary also names the island tenant, Major Peter Wood.
rows.summary: The island and its history has been depicted in a number of works of literature: the author Compton Mackenzie, who was the island tenant 1920–23, represented it in Fairy Gold, albeit in a fictional portrayal. Jenny Wood, the wife of tenant Major Peter Wood, published her memoirs in 1986.

rows.title: Peter Calvay, Hermit: A Personal Rediscovery of Prayer
rows.evidence: The specialist in mystical theology and author Rayner Torkington wrote a novel concerning Christian Mysticism featuring a character based on his late brother Peter Torkington called Peter Calvay, whom in the novel had lived on the island of Hellisay for a number of years in the first half of the twentieth century.
rows.summary: The specialist in mystical theology and author Rayner Torkington wrote a novel concerning Christian Mysticism featuring a character based on his late brother Peter Torkington called Peter Calvay, whom in the novel had lived on the island of Hellisay for a number of years in the first half of the twentieth century. The book, titled Peter Calvay, Hermit: A Personal Rediscovery of Prayer, was first published in 1977 and has had at least eleven reprintings.

rows.title: Wisdom from the Western Isles: The Making of a Mystic
rows.evidence: Torkington's novel Wisdom from the Western Isles: The Making of a Mystic, published in 2008, also describes the author's meetings with Peter Calvay whilst he was staying on Barra.
rows.summary: Torkington's novel Wisdom from the Western Isles: The Making of a Mystic, published in 2008, also describes the author's meetings with Peter Calvay whilst he was staying on Barra.

rows.title: Magnus
rows.evidence: The story returns to 12th-century Orkney, and concludes with the tinkers, Jock and Mary (present since the outset of the tale).
rows.reject_reason: The article's sentences in the summary place Magnus in Orkney and call him Earl of Orkney. They do not set the novel on Mainland.
rows.summary: Magnus is a novel by the Orcadian author George Mackay Brown. His second novel, it was published in 1973. it is a fictional account of the life and execution of the 12th-century saint, Magnus Erlendsson, Earl of Orkney. The story returns to 12th-century Orkney, and concludes with the tinkers, Jock and Mary (present since the outset of the tale).

rows.title: The Golden Bird
rows.evidence: Brown later formed an intense, platonic attachment to Kenna Crawford, to whom he dedicated The Golden Bird: Two Orkney Stories and some poems in the volume The wreck of the Archangel.
rows.reject_reason: The article's sentence says Brown dedicated The Golden Bird: Two Orkney Stories to Kenna Crawford. It does not set those stories on Mainland.
rows.summary: Brown later formed an intense, platonic attachment to Kenna Crawford, to whom he dedicated The Golden Bird: Two Orkney Stories and some poems in the volume The wreck of the Archangel.

rows.title: The Lost Lights of St Kilda
rows.evidence: The story of St Kilda has attracted artistic interpretations, including Michael Powell's 1937 film The Edge of the World, the novel The Lost Lights of St Kilda by Elisabeth Gifford, and an opera.
rows.reject_reason: The St Kilda article lists the novel among artistic interpretations of the story of St Kilda, in the same sentence as a film and an opera. It does not say the novel is set on the island.
rows.summary: The story of St Kilda has attracted artistic interpretations, including Michael Powell's 1937 film The Edge of the World, the novel The Lost Lights of St Kilda by Elisabeth Gifford, and an opera.

rows.title: Frankenstein
rows.evidence: Victor and his friend Henry Clerval leave the European mainland for Britain, where Victor establishes a laboratory in Orkney.
rows.reject_reason: The article says Victor establishes a laboratory in Orkney. It does not name Mainland.
rows.summary: Frankenstein; or, The Modern Prometheus is an 1818 Gothic novel written by English author Mary Shelley. Victor and his friend Henry Clerval leave the European mainland for Britain, where Victor establishes a laboratory in Orkney.
